reader.title: Pensacola and Atlantic Railroad camp shooting (1881)
bases: In the fuller local account a white man beaten in a camp quarrel gathered a crowd that watched a Black worker's camp for several nights before it was fired into and a colored man killed (A1); the wire brief instead blames 'the other negroes' for the firing (A2).

Both reports agree that a quarrel between Turnage and a colored man at the English camp ended in night firing into a camp and the death of a colored man, but A1 implies Turnage's crowd fired into Bradwell's camp while A2 says the other negroes fired into the camp (A1, A2).

summary.text: The Pensacola and Atlantic Railroad camp shooting was a night shooting in late October 1881 at Mr. English Albert's railroad camp in Florida that killed a colored man from Georgia and slightly wounded three others.
It followed a quarrel between a white man named Turnage and a Black worker, and the two surviving reports disagree on who fired.
According to the Quincy Herald, the trouble began when Turnage, a white man from Georgia, defended a boy whom Caesar Bradwell, "a colored man from this county," was "chunking at" for awkward work.
Other Black workers joined in, and Turnage fetched a horse pistol, but its caps had been removed.
Several men then beat him with shovels and spades.
Turnage afterwards gathered a crowd of men "from some source unknown," and for several nights they watched Bradwell's camp.
Bradwell had left but came back on a Thursday night, and that night his camp was fired into.
The shots killed a colored man from Georgia, apparently also described as Turnage's friend and companion, and slightly wounded three others.
A coroner's inquest was held over the dead man, but the Herald had not heard the verdict.
No report of arrests or a trial appears in the coverage.

The Savannah Morning News reprinted the Herald item on 3 November in its column of Florida news, where it referred to the Black workers as "darkies" and said its account came from "persons engaged in working the railroad."
On 7 November the Omaha Daily Bee ran an Associated Press brief from Columbus, Georgia, headed "A Row in Camp".
That brief named the Black man in the quarrel Quinley and did not mention Turnage's crowd.
The Herald never says who fired, but its account points to the crowd that Turnage gathered to watch Bradwell's camp.
The Columbus dispatch says instead that "the other negroes" fired into the camp, killing a colored man and wounding others.
The Herald's wording also leaves unclear whether one or two men died, though it mentions an inquest over a single dead man.

accounts.label: Quincy Herald (from railroad workers)
accounts.gist: After Turnage was beaten with shovels and spades, he gathered a crowd that watched Bradwell's camp for several nights; the camp was fired into the night Bradwell returned, killing a colored man from Georgia and wounding three slightly. The paper does not say who fired.

accounts.label: Wire report (Columbus, Ga.)
accounts.gist: Turnage and a colored man named Quinley quarreled; the other negroes took it up and fired into the camp at night, killing a colored man and wounding others.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News reprinted the Quincy Herald item in its Florida news column; the item used 'darkies' and 'the negro', blamed Bradwell for starting the quarrel, said Turnage's crowd came 'from some source unknown', and noted that it was secondhand.
The Omaha Daily Bee ran a short Associated Press brief, 'A Row in Camp', among crime items, saying the Black workers did the shooting.

info: The quarrel occurred 'last week' and the camp was fired into on a Thursday night, per the Quincy Herald as reprinted on 3 November 1881; the date is therefore late October 1881 (inferred).

The camp of Mr. English Albert (A1) or Mr. English (A2) on the Pensacola and Atlantic Railroad in Florida; the item came from the Quincy Herald, which called Bradwell 'a colored man from this county'.

Bradwell's camp was the reported target; the dead man was an unnamed colored man from Georgia, possibly also described as Turnage's friend and companion; three other parties slightly wounded, race not stated.
No crime accusation; the quarrel began when Turnage defended a boy whom Bradwell was 'chunking at' for awkward work, after which several Black workers beat Turnage with shovels and spades.

Contested: the Quincy Herald does not name the shooters but says Turnage gathered a crowd of men that watched Bradwell's camp for several nights before it was fired into; the wire brief says 'the other negroes' fired into the camp.

sources.note: Florida news column quoting the Quincy Herald: quarrel between Turnage (white, from Georgia) and Caesar Bradwell (colored, of the county) at Mr. English Albert's railroad camp; Turnage beaten, then gathered a crowd that watched Bradwell's camp; camp fired into, a death and three slightly wounded; inquest held.
quotes: Turnage afterwards gathered up a crowd of men, from some source unknown, and for several nights they watched the camp of the colored man, Bradwell.
His camp was fired into the same night, resulting in the death of a colored man from Georgia and the friend and companion of Turnage who had not been engaged in the trouble
A Coroner's inquest was held over the dead man, but we have not heard the verdict.
